Sub-protocol B: Valemetostat in combination with T-DXd in subjects with previously treated, advanced or metastatic HER2-positive gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma; for details, see Sub-protocol B. Sub-protocol C: Valemetostat in combination with Dato-DXd in subjects with previously treated, locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic non-squamous NSCLC with or without actionable genomic alteration(s); for details, see Sub-protocol C.

A phase 2 study of ianalumab (VAY736) in patients with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) previously treated with at least two lines of therapies
conditions: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is a rare, acquired, immune-mediated disease of adults and children, characterized by transient or persistent decrease of the platelet count and, depending upon the degree of thrombocytopenia, increased risk of bleeding. Primary ITP is defined by the absence of other causes or disorders that may be associated with thrombocytopenia. Secondary forms include thrombocytopenias that are due to an underlying disease or to drug exposure. The pathophysiology of ITP is characterized by both an increased peripheral destruction of platelets together with an inappropriate platelet production in the bone marrow due to the immune response being also directed against megakaryocytes. Although the factors triggering primary ITP remain unknown, autoreactive splenic B-cells differentiating into antiplatelet antibody-producing plasma cells have a key role. These autoantibodies directed against different glycoproteins on the surface of platelets and megakaryocytes mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity. Most commonly, ITP patients have asymptomatic thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 G/L) and significant bleeding rarely occurs with platelet count levels 30 G/L. ITP patients usually seek medical help once bleeding symptoms occur. While most hemorrhages are mild, presenting with bruising and petechiae, severe hemorrhages involving the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract are well known complications of the disease, and occur in approximately 10% of adult ITP patients. The most serious and life-threatening bleeding complications are intracranial hemorrhages reported to occurred in 1.4% of adults with ITP. The frequency of death from hemorrhage in patients with platelet counts <30 G/L is estimated to be between 1.6 and 3.9 per 100 patient-year, although the frequency is influenced by age, severity, and duration of thrombocytopenia.

conditions: La esteatohepatitis no alcohólica (EHNA) es la forma progresiva de la enfermedad del hígado graso no alcohólico (EHGNA) con una prevalencia de aproximadamente el 2 % al 3 % de la población general. La esteatohepatitis no alcohólica puede provocar cirrosis y sus complicaciones, carcinoma hepatocelular y enfermedad hepática en etapa terminal. La esteatohepatitis no alcohólica se define histológicamente como una condición multicomponente compuesta por esteatosis hepática, inflamación y balonización de hepatocitos en proporciones variables. La EHNA se diferencia de la esteatosis por la presencia de inflamación y lesión de las células hepáticas en respuesta a lipotóxicos intermedios que se acumulan y metabolizan en el hígado esteatósico. La EHNA está estrechamente relacionada con factores de riesgo metabólicos, como la obesidad, la DM2 y la dislipidemia. Fisiopatologicamente, la EHNA se asocia frecuentemente con un estado hiperinsulinémico o resistente a la insulina, lo que lleva a una disfunción del tejido adiposo y a un aumento del deterioro hepático de nueva lipogénesis

"Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatatis (NASH) is the progressive form of Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)with a prevalence of approximately 2% to 3% of the general population. Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis can lead to cirrhosis and its complications, hepatocellular carcinoma, and end stage liver disease. Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis is defined histologically as a multicomponent condition composed of hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning in varying proportions. NASH differs from steatosis alone by the presence of hepatic cell inflammation and injury in response to lipotoxic intermediates that are accumulated and metabolized in the steatotic liver. NASH is closely associated with metabolic risk factors including obesity, T2DM, and dyslipidemia. Pathophysiologically, NASH is frequently associated with a hyperinsulinemic or insulin resistant state, leading to adipose tissue dysfunction and increased hepatic de novo lipogenesis."<br/
